html:
The Aymara kingdoms, or Aymara lordships, were native states around Lake Titicaca in the high Andes, in what is now Peru and Bolivia. They rose after the fall of Tiwanaku, from about 1150, and lasted until the Inca conquered them, a process complete by about 1477.

The best known were the Colla, north and west of the lake, and the Lupaca, on its southwestern shore; others included the Pacajes, Charcas and Carangas. They spoke Aymara and Puquina. Their wealth was in herds of llama and alpaca and in crops of the high plain such as potatoes and quinoa. Their lords built fortified hilltop towns and stone burial towers called chullpas, like those at Sillustani.

Colla and Lupaca were rivals, and the Inca used that rivalry. Pachacuti and his successors brought the lake under Inca rule in the 1400s. Today about two million Aymara people live in Bolivia, Peru, Chile and Argentina. See also Andean states and chiefdoms.
